newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: U.S. says Iran tests air-launched missiles in Gulf.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iran tests air-launched missiles in Gulf.

text.p: Iran this month successfully tested air-launched Chinese-made cruise missiles in the Gulf, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Tuesday.

"Recently it successfully tested an air-launched anti-ship cruise missile. Iran's word and action suggests that it wants to be able to intimidate neighbours and interrupt commerce in the Gulf," Cohen told a news conference in Bahrain.
"The United States will not allow this to happen," he said.
Asked what kind of missiles Iran tested, Cohen said: "Chinese missiles".
"The United States retains overwhelming naval strength in the Gulf and we are fully capable of protecting our ships, our interests and our allies," he said.

Asked whether the new missiles posed a threat to U.S. forces in the region, Cohen said: "Any time any nation acquires new technology it causes us to watch it very closely. But we are convinced and have no doubt that we have the capability to defeat any weapon system that Iran might possess."

Cohen, who is on a tour of five Gulf Arab states, said Iran "continues to support terrorism in addition to developing weapons of mass destruction, improving missiles that can strike neighbouring nations and boosting the facility to close the Strait of Hormuz".
"In the last two years, Iran has concentrated on developing a more robust anti-ship missile capability and has deployed anti-ship cruise missiles on the shores," he added.
U.S. defence officials told Reuters Iran tested the Chinese C-801 missiles from an F-4 fighter jet on June 3 and June 6. "Both tests were very successful," one said.
"The test on the third of June tested the guidance system and the one on the sixth tested the conventional warhead," the official added.
The U.S. officials said the tests, the first such successful launches by Iran, enhanced Iran's capability in the region and added a new dimension to regional threats.

The United States, which accuses Iran of sponsoring state terrorism -- a charge Iran denies -- has expressed growing concern since the 1991 Gulf War about what it describes as Iran's growing military capability and its aims in the region.
Iran opposes the U.S. military presence in the Gulf and says Washington falsely accuses Tehran of threatening regional security in order to scare its Gulf Arab allies into buying more U.S. weapons.
The Iranian navy fired a Chinese-built C-802 anti-ship missile from one of its 10 Houdong patrol boats during exercises in the Gulf last November.

U.S. officials had said Iran's acquisition of the radar-guided C-802 missiles, which they expect to be operational on about 20 Iranian vessels, was a new dimension in the naval threat in the oil-rich region.
China earlier this month defended what it called transfers of small amounts of conventional weapons to Iran, describing them as appropriate and legal.
U.S. press reports had said that China sold Iran missile technology, advanced radar components and nearly 400 tonnes of chemicals used to produce nerve agents.
